back: Single bespoke products or prototypes. The user gets an original product, but it needs lots of manual labour.
Limited numbers of similar items made at one time, possibly repeated. There may be a delay until the next batch.
Identical products made in large volume with automated machinery. More profit, but high set-up costs and little flexibility.
Identical products made 24/7 on heavily automated lines — huge numbers efficiently, but one fault can stop the whole process.
Drinks cans, plastic bottles, bottle caps, screws and fixings, newspapers and food packaging.
A device that holds material and guides cutting or drilling tools for accuracy and repeatability.
A tool for marking out the same shape repeatedly.
Faster and more accurate than by hand, consistent repeats, multiple items at once, less waste, and can work without supervision.
Granules from a hopper are carried by a screw through a heated barrel and melted; the screw rams the polymer into a closed, cooled mould; it cools under pressure; ejector pins push the product out.
Very fast cycles, complex 3D shapes in one piece, identical accurate products, self-finishing, little waste.
Very expensive moulds (only economical in large quantities), design changes need a new mould, walls must be even, draft angles needed.

front: How to spot an injection-moulded product
back: Circular ejector pin marks, a sprue mark, tapered sides (draft angles) and strengthening ribs inside.
A soft plastic tube is inflated to fill a mould cavity — used for bottles.
A heated sheet of HIPS or acrylic is pulled over a mould by sucking the air out.
Polymer is placed in a heated mould cavity, then compressed by a plug in a hydraulic press.
High-volume printing where oil-based ink sticks to the image area of a plate and water to the rest; the image is offset onto a rubber blanket, then the paper.
Cyan, magenta, yellow and key (black) — the four inks used to build up colour images.
Offset: high quality and cheap per item for long runs, but slow and expensive to set up. Digital printing is used for short runs.
Metal cutters stamp the required shape (e.g. a package net) out of card.
